cover.headline: A rare fermentation-API franchise coming out of a lost year: Concord's own short history gives 61x Sep-28E EPS, the price pays 34x: target {{dcf.tp|inr}}, BUY on the house rule, with low conviction
cover.lead: Concord Biotech grows microbes in 1,250 m³ of fermenters in Gujarat to make active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) few others can: immunosuppressants for transplant patients (tacrolimus, mycophenolate, cyclosporine; 58% of revenue), oncology and anti-infective molecules, 79% of revenue in all, plus formulations (21%), now including a new injectable plant. FY26 revenue fell 12% and EPS 30% to ₹24.9 as customers deferred orders, EU supplies stalled on a regulatory approval and two tenders were lost; Q1FY27 revenue rose 26%. We forecast EPS of ₹29.1 / 36.6 / 43.5 for FY27-29E. Both brokers that disclose a method use **P/E**, and so do we: Concord's median one-year-forward P/E since 1-Jan-2024 (54.9x; listed Aug-2023, post-listing months skipped), lifted 10.7% for the pharma peers' move over the same window, gives **61x Sep-28E EPS of ₹40.0 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY**. That median is inflated by FY26: the year the market priced on FY26 EPS reads 67.9x; leaving it out gives 47.5x (₹1,900), still a BUY. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹2,259; DCF ₹695, which says the cash flows do not support even today's price. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}. Per-share figures are before the 1:1 bonus approved on 23-Sep-2026.

arguments.p: 1,250 m³ of fermentation capacity, 30+ fermentation APIs, a 20%+ global volume share in five molecules, approvals from the USFDA, EU, Japan, Korea and Brazil, 300+ customers (top ten only 37.6%), no debt and ₹442 cr of cash. Gross margins of 74-79% show limited competition.

arguments.h: But mature molecules and lumpy buyers
arguments.p: Immunosuppressants are 74% of API revenue; tacrolimus and mycophenolate are decades-old generics. FY26 showed that customers can defer orders for quarters, and Q1FY27's share gains were "primarily driven by pricing". FY25's EPS of ₹35.5 returns only in FY28E on our numbers.

arguments.h: New bets cost margin for now
arguments.p: The injectable plant (₹600 cr peak revenue) runs at ~5% utilisation and the US front end (Stellon, 75% owned) has just started selling: together ~₹48 cr of costs, 4-5 points of margin. Management targets ~40% EBITDA in FY28; we assume 38%. Cash may also go to acquisitions in "adjacencies".

arguments.h: A mechanical BUY, not a strong one
arguments.p: ₹1,374 is 52.2x trailing EPS and 37.5x our FY28E. Our rule reads 3 years of history in which the stock traded at 28-104x the EPS that came in; the street's P/E users sit at 25-40x FY28E (40x gives ₹1,600), the latest targets cluster at ₹1,190-1,645 (median ₹1,400), and the DCF needs ~24% growth for 15 years.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): our FY27 needs Q2-Q4 revenue 15% above a year earlier; Q4 orders decide the year.
1:1 bonus: shareholder approval and a record date still to come (board approval 23-Sep-2026); no change to value.
Injectables: first third-party contract-manufacturing orders expected in H2FY27; emerging-market registrations take 12-15 months.
CDMO: at least one more innovator project expected to convert in FY27 (today 1-2% of revenue).
Middle East and US Veterans Affairs tenders (~₹25 cr each) still on hold; any return is upside to formulations.
USFDA: closure of the one procedural observation at the Valthera formulation plant (inspection ended 18-Sep-2026).
Capital allocation: management is "exploring" acquisitions in fermentation adjacencies (peptides, veterinary).

sections.title: What Concord does: fermentation APIs for transplant, cancer and infection medicines (79% of revenue), and the formulations made from them (21%)

blocks.p: Most APIs are made by chemistry. Concord makes a narrower set by **fermentation**: it grows selected strains of bacteria or fungi in large steel tanks for 30-50 days, then extracts and purifies the molecule they produce (ICRA). The process is slow, capital-heavy and hard to scale, so few companies outside China and Europe do it at size. Concord has 1,250 m³ of fermenters at two API plants near Ahmedabad, 30+ fermentation APIs and 150+ drug master files (DMFs) filed around the world, and says it holds a 20%+ global volume share in five molecules. In FY26 APIs brought ₹828.8 cr (79% of revenue) and formulations ₹226.1 cr (21%).

blocks.p: **Who buys.** Concord sells APIs to 300+ generic drug makers in 70+ countries, including the regulated markets (US, Europe, Japan) through its DMFs. "Domestic" sales (₹563.8 cr in FY26, 53%) are largely to Indian formulators who export the finished drug, so the US matters more than its direct US sales (₹108.0 cr, 10%) suggest: management calls most of its US business "indirect". The top ten customers were 37.6% of FY26 revenue (48.2% in FY21) and no customer reaches 10% (AR FY26). Concord does not disclose a regulated vs emerging-market split, customer names or molecule revenues.

**What is new.** Three businesses are being built on top of the API base: (1) **injectables** (Unit IV, commercial since Mar-2025, ₹600 cr peak revenue potential, ~5% utilised); (2) **Stellon Biotech Inc.**, a 75%-owned US company that started selling Concord's (and in-licensed) formulations in Q1FY27; (3) **CDMO**, contract work on innovators' molecules (1-2% of revenue; one animal-health product commercial). Management sees ₹3,000 cr of revenue from today's plants in 5-6 years (₹2,200-2,300 cr APIs, ₹600-700 cr formulations), almost three times FY26.

blocks.callout: **So what:** this is a specialist API maker whose profits come from a handful of mature, hard-to-make molecules, sold to generic companies that can and do switch timing. The fermentation know-how is real; the formulation and injectable add-ons are still a cost, not a profit, and their payoff is a forecast.

blocks.p: **Corporate actions that matter for per-share data.** In Jul-2022 Concord split its ₹10 shares into ten ₹1 shares and issued one bonus share for every ten (AR FY26 note 16), taking the count to 10.46 cr. On 23-Sep-2026, a week before our as-of date, the board approved a **1:1 bonus** (its first as a listed company), subject to shareholder approval, and raised authorised capital from ₹11 cr to ₹22 cr. The bonus changes the number of shares, not the value of the company. Every per-share figure in this report (price ₹1,373.6, EPS, DPS, target) is on the 10.46 cr shares in issue on 30-Sep-2026; after the bonus, halve them.

**Acquisitions and overseas moves (all small, verified in AR FY26).** Stellon Biotech Inc. (USA, 75% from 1-Jul-2025); Concord Lifegen Ltd (India, 100%, Jul-2025, domestic formulations); Celliimune Biotech Pvt Ltd (cell and gene therapy research, 100% from 2-Apr-2026 for ₹66 lakh, bought from director Ravi Kapoor); 26% of Clean Max Everglades (₹6.1 cr, captive solar power, Jan-2025); 71,472 shares of Palvella Therapeutics Inc. (US biotech; ₹84.1 cr fair value at Mar-26); and the 50% Japan JV (since Oct-2019). None is material to revenue yet. Management says it is exploring acquisitions in "adjacencies" of fermentation (peptides, veterinary products) with its cash.

blocks.callout: **So what:** Concord has funded every plant from its own cash; the IPO was an exit for Quadria Capital, which sold its entire 20% (₹1,550.5 cr at ₹741 a share). The recent acquisitions are tiny, but they show where the cash pile could go next.

sections.title: Fermentation APIs: a slow-growing, high-barrier corner of the API market, dominated by a few Chinese, European and Indian makers

blocks.p: About 30% of the world's APIs by value are biological rather than synthetic (Fortune Business Insights, cited in AR FY26), and the microbial (fermentation) API market is growing ~6.7% a year to 2030. The barriers are physical and technical: large sterile fermenters, strains that must be improved for years to give a commercial yield, long cycles and heavy working capital, plus regulatory approval for every site and molecule. That keeps the number of credible suppliers per molecule small, which is why Concord's gross margin (after materials) has stayed at 74-79%. The flip side is that the molecules are old: tacrolimus, mycophenolate and cyclosporine have been generic for years, demand grows slowly, with the number of patients on lifelong therapy, and each new supplier usually wins share on price.

blocks.p: **Competition.** Concord does not name its competitors. Its own decks describe fusidic acid as having "limited competition mainly from European manufacturers", and its new launches enter "as a second source" at "an aggressive price". In India the other large fermentation API maker is Biocon (its generics business makes several of the same immunosuppressants and statins); Biocon trades at 82.9x trailing EPS, distorted by its biologics business. Most listed Indian API makers (Divi's, Laurus, Granules, Neuland) are mostly chemistry-based.

blocks.callout: **So what:** the industry gives Concord pricing power through scarcity, not growth. Its growth has to come from taking share (often on price), launching the next niche molecule every year, and moving into formulations, injectables and contract work.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the tailwind Concord is best placed for is the one it has always had, being one of few qualified fermentation suppliers. The newer tailwinds (CDMO, injectables, the US front end) are where its growth story points, but in Q1FY27 they were still costs. We give them some credit in FY28-29E formulation growth (+18-20%), not in the multiple.

sections.title: APIs: ₹829 cr in FY26 (−12%), +42% in Q1FY27; growth is now coming from oncology and anti-infectives, and from lower prices

blocks.p: API revenue grew from ₹761 cr (FY23) to ₹940 cr (FY25), then fell 12% to ₹828.8 cr in FY26: management says volumes fell and prices were flat ("there has been no price growth for us... it has been primarily on the basis of volume", Q4FY26 call). Q1FY27 API revenue rose 42% to ₹218.9 cr. The growth was "broad-based": every therapy grew by double digits, with oncology and anti-infectives "much, much more" than immunosuppressants, helped by new products (Nystatin, launched in FY25, and fusidic acid, launched in FY26), new customers and FY26 orders spilling over.

pair.title: API revenue: ₹761 cr (FY23) to ₹940 cr (FY25), ₹829 cr (FY26)
Quarterly API revenue: Q4FY25 ₹362 cr, Q1FY26 ₹154 cr, Q1FY27 ₹219 cr

blocks.h: Concentration: by therapy high, by customer moderate

blocks.p: **By therapy**, Concord is concentrated: immunosuppressants were 74% of FY26 API revenue and 58% of total revenue (ICRA, 23-Sep-2026), and its key products are tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and mycophenolate sodium (ICRA). At the IPO the top five molecules were a large share of revenue; management declined to update that figure on the Q4FY26 call ("last year would not be a right year to look into what the top 5 molecules has contributed"). **By customer**, it is diversified: 300+ customers, the top ten 37.6% of revenue (down from 48.2% in FY21) and none above 10%.

Concord does not disclose prices by molecule, so we rely on management's words. On mature products "there is always a little bit of price that to certain customers could be there, which gets compensated by the newer regions" (Q4FY26 call). New products enter "as a second source" with "an aggressive price". And Q1FY27's wallet-share gains at existing customers were "primarily driven by pricing": Concord uses its scale (1,250 m³) to undercut competitors while "still able to maintain our healthy profitability margins". Gross margin (78.9% in Q1FY27, 76.7% in FY26) has not shown erosion yet; the rupee (~10-12% weaker) added ~3-5 points to Q1FY27 growth. Our reading: volume growth bought with price is a sound strategy for a low-cost producer, but it caps the margin upside.

sections.title: Formulations: ₹226 cr in FY26 and −23% in Q1FY27; the injectable plant and the US front end are costs waiting for revenue

blocks.p: Concord began making finished doses in FY2016 at Valthera to use its own APIs (backward integration). Formulation revenue grew from ₹92 cr (FY23) to ₹260 cr (FY25, +38%), then fell 13% to ₹226.1 cr in FY26 and 23% to ₹38.6 cr in Q1FY27. The fall is mostly geopolitics: a Middle East government tender (~₹25 cr of formulations) has been on hold since Q3FY26, the US Veterans Affairs tender (~₹25 cr) was not finalised, and some Middle East buyers switched to buying Concord's API (longer shelf life) instead of tablets. Management says that excluding the Middle East its domestic divisions (nephrology and critical care) grew by double digits.

blocks.p: **The cost of the ramp-up.** The capex is done: gross block rose from ₹826 cr (Mar-24) to ₹1,161 cr (Mar-26), mostly the injectable plant, and FY26 capex fell to ₹65 cr (CFO; ₹95 cr on Screener's cash-flow basis). What is not done is filling it. The injectable plant cost ~₹38-39 cr in FY26 and Stellon ~₹10 cr, together ~4.6% of revenue, before meaningful sales; depreciation rose from ₹54 cr (FY25) to ₹74.5 cr (FY26). Management guides maintenance capex of ₹20-30 cr a year plus a small topical facility in FY27, a ₹50-100 cr debottlenecking in 2-3 years, and a Unit III expansion only when utilisation reaches 80-85%. ICRA (Sep-2026) is less sanguine and puts FY27 capex at ₹120-130 cr; we use ₹100 cr, ₹90 cr and ₹110 cr for FY27-29E.

blocks.callout: **So what:** Concord does not need money to grow for several years; it needs orders. Every 10 points of utilisation at the injectable plant is ~₹60 cr of revenue against a cost base already paid for, which is why the margin could recover fast if the orders come, and why it has stayed down while they have not. The regulatory record (no warning letter found; the 2025 and 2026 USFDA inspections ended with procedural observations only) is a real asset.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict: a narrow but real moat.** Few companies can make these molecules at this scale and pass USFDA, EU and Japanese inspections, and 74-79% gross margins prove it. But the moat protects old molecules, not growth: Concord must keep cutting prices to win share and launching niche products to replace erosion, and the businesses it is adding (formulations, injectables, US marketing) have no moat of their own beyond owning the API.

sections.title: Q4 is the big quarter, Q1 the small one; FY26 swapped bulk Q4 orders for staggered quarterly buying

blocks.p: Concord's customers (generic formulators and a few innovators) buy APIs in campaigns, and many place their largest orders before their own financial year-end: Q4 brought 31% of revenue in FY24 and 36% in FY25 (₹430 cr), while Q1 is usually the smallest quarter. In FY26 customers "shifted from bulk purchases to a more staggered quarter-on-quarter procurement approach" (Q4FY26 call): Q4FY26 revenue fell 24% to ₹326 cr even though Q3FY26 grew 14%. Margins follow revenue because ~45-50% of costs (employees 17%, power and fuel ~20% of costs) are fixed: the EBITDA margin ranged from 30% (Q1FY26) to 44% (Q4FY25).

pair.title: Quarterly revenue: Q4FY25 ₹430 cr, Q1FY26 ₹204 cr
Quarterly EBITDA margin: 30% to 44%

blocks.callout: **What to watch:** our FY27 forecast (₹1,232 cr) needs ₹975 cr from Q2-Q4 after Q1's ₹257.5 cr, 15% above the same quarters of FY26 (₹851 cr). The whole year hinges on Q4: whether customers return to bulk year-end orders or keep buying quarterly. Q2FY27 results are due by mid-November 2026.

sections.title: Eight years of high-teens growth at 40%+ margins, then FY26: revenue −12%, EBITDA −27%, EPS ₹35.5 to ₹24.9

blocks.p: Concord's revenue grew from ₹340 cr in FY18 to ₹1,200 cr in FY25, ~20% a year, with the EBITDA margin at 37-53% (40-42% in FY23-25) and almost no debt. The only dip before FY26 was FY22 (EPS ₹22.5 to ₹16.7), when the new Limbasi API plant (Unit III) added ~₹22 cr of depreciation and start-up costs before it had volume. **FY26 broke the pattern:** revenue fell 12% to ₹1,055 cr, EBITDA 27% to ₹368 cr and EPS 30% to ₹24.9. Three things hit at once: US customers bought in small quarterly lots instead of bulk, EU supplies stopped for ~3 months while the regulator's written confirmation was pending, and Middle East and US Veterans Affairs tenders (~₹25 cr each) did not happen. On top, the new injectable plant and the US front end (Stellon Biotech) added ~₹48 cr of costs with little revenue. EPS figures are on the 10.46 cr shares that traded on 30-Sep-2026 (before the 1:1 bonus approved on 23-Sep-2026 and not yet allotted).

bullets: **Cash conversion is good.** Operating cash flow was ₹267 cr in FY26, 102% of profit, and ~88% over FY21-26, despite rising working capital.

**Other income is 15% of FY26 pre-tax profit**: treasury gains ₹23.6 cr, forex ₹16.0 cr (₹8.2 cr in FY25), Gujarat incentives ₹7.9 cr. We forecast no forex gains. Screener treats ₹15.0 cr after tax of FY26 profit as "exceptional" (EPS ₹1.4); the company's only exceptional item is the ₹3.3 cr labour-code charge.

**The Palvella gain bypasses profit.** Concord's shares in Palvella Therapeutics rose from ₹17.3 cr to ₹84.1 cr in FY26; the gain went to other comprehensive income (FY26 OCI ₹55.2 cr), so it does not flatter EPS, but it is also volatile and unhedged.

**Inventory needs watching.** Inventory rose 36% to ₹326 cr while revenue fell 12%; management says it is API stock for staggered orders, not formulations, and sees "very low" write-off risk. Work in progress (₹194 cr) is the bulk of it (AR FY26 note 27).
**Minority and EPS basis.** Stellon's loss is shared with a 25% partner; we use profit attributable to owners (₹260.9 cr, ₹24.94 a share). The AR's EPS of ₹24.78 divides total profit by shares.
**Auditor and segments.** B S R & Co. LLP (KPMG network), unqualified; one reported segment, so API and formulation margins are not disclosed.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Simple accounts, real cash; intangible assets under development are only ₹1.2 cr, so R&D is expensed. The judgement calls are working capital and how much of other income is market gains.

sections.title: No debt and ₹442 cr of cash (Jun-26), but working capital swallowed 61% of FY26 sales as inventory rose to ₹326 cr

blocks.p: Concord has had no meaningful debt since FY24 and held ₹415.7 cr of cash and debt funds at Mar-26 (>₹442 cr at Jun-26), plus ₹84.1 cr of shares in Palvella Therapeutics, a US biotech, and ₹3.7 cr in its Japan JV. The weak spot is working capital. Fermentation takes 30-50 days, the last 1-5% of processing waits for an order, and customers get 115-120 days of credit (ICRA): working capital was ~53% of sales in FY25 and 63% in FY26 (ICRA). In FY26 inventory rose from ₹240 cr to ₹326 cr (485 days of material cost) as customers deferred orders, while receivables fell from ₹522 cr to ₹460 cr. Operating cash flow was still ₹267 cr and free cash flow ~₹172 cr (Screener), most of it paid out (₹112 cr of dividends) or parked in debt funds.

blocks.p: Concord funded Limbasi, the injectable plant and the new subsidiaries from its own cash flow, paid ~30% of profit as dividends since listing (FY26: ₹7.55 a share, 30%) and parked the rest in debt funds. That kept the balance sheet debt-free but diluted returns: cash and funds were ~25% of FY26 net worth. ROE was 13.6% in FY26 against a 12.5% cost of equity. On our forecasts ROE recovers to {{F.roe.0|pct}} / {{F.roe.1|pct}} / {{F.roe.2|pct}} in FY27-29E, still below FY23-25's 20-22%, because cash keeps building (₹877 cr by Mar-29E) and working capital stays at ~61% of sales.

blocks.callout: **Capital allocation risk:** management is "looking at different inorganic growth strategies" in fermentation adjacencies (peptides, veterinary) and has started small (Celliimune, Stellon, Palvella). A large acquisition in an unfamiliar field is the main way this clean balance sheet could go wrong; a higher payout or buyback would be the shareholder-friendly alternative, and management mentions dividends only as "historically" paid.

sections.title: Ownership: the Vaid family owns 44.1% and the Jhunjhunwala trusts 24.1%; Quadria sold its entire 20% in the IPO

blocks.p: **Who owns Concord (Jun-2026).** The Vaid family holds 44.08%: chairman and MD Sudhir Vaid 28.84%, his wife Manju Vaid 9.55%, Sudman Consultants LLP 4.54%, JMD and CEO Ankur Vaid 0.56%. The three Jhunjhunwala family discretionary trusts (Rekha Jhunjhunwala, trustee) hold 24.09% between them (8.03% each); they are public, not promoter, shareholders. Foreign institutions hold 7.53%, domestic institutions 9.37% and ~83,325 shareholders the rest. The IPO (Aug-2023) was a 100% offer for sale by Helix Investment Holdings (Quadria Capital), which sold its entire 20% at ₹741 a share (₹1,550.5 cr); anchor investors took ₹465 cr.

sections.title: Management & governance: a capable founder family and a clean regulatory record; some related-party habits and a CEO-chairman structure

blocks.p: Concord is run by its founder, Sudhir Vaid (chairman and MD, ~five decades in biotechnology; he took over the loss-making unit in 2000), and his son Ankur Vaid (joint MD and CEO, who leads the calls). A new CFO, Raviraj Karia, joined in Q3FY26. The board has nine directors: the two Vaids, two non-independent non-executives (Ravi Kapoor, Rajiv Agarwal) and five independents. The two executive promoters were paid ₹11.0 cr in FY26 (₹7.07 cr and ₹3.91 cr, 111.9x and 66.3x the median employee), 4.2% of attributable profit, with no increase while profit fell 30%.

sections.title: Valuation: 61x Sep-28E EPS gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} (BUY); the price pays 34x, the street 25-40x, and the DCF says ₹695

blocks.p: The two brokers whose method we could see both use **P/E on FY28E EPS**: Choice 40x (Add, ₹1,645, 4-Aug-2026) and Antique 25x (Buy, ₹1,520, 6-Jan-2026). Kotak (Buy), Citi and Jefferies (Hold) do not disclose a method in the summaries we found. We therefore value on **P/E on Sep-28E EPS (half FY28E, half FY29E)**, with EV/EBITDA and a DCF as cross-checks, never weights. Concord has no debt and our forecasts carry no exceptional items or forex gains.

Concord listed on 18-Aug-2023 (issue price ₹741, first close ₹943), so there is no five-year history and the batch rule for recent listings applies (PLAYBOOK §7c): skip the post-listing months and pair the own window with the peers' move over the same window. On the chart, the post-listing phase is clear: the stock re-rated almost every week from ₹943 to ₹1,505 by 22-Dec-2023 (forward P/E 26.5x to 42.4x, median 32.7x), then moved sideways at ₹1,395-1,560 for the next five months. By 1-Jan-2024 the 90-day anchor lock-in had ended (Nov-2023) and the company had reported two quarters as a listed company. **We start the window on 1-Jan-2024** (144 points: every weekly close plus the 30-Sep-2026 close). Unusually, skipping the listing months raises the median rather than lowering it, because Concord listed cheap and re-rated afterwards; starting at listing gives 56.5x, from 1-Nov-2023 59x, from 1-Mar-2024 (after the six-month pre-IPO lock-in) 63x, all with the peers' move over the same window. **Every one of these is a BUY.**

Forward P/E = price ÷ the next full fiscal year's EPS as it actually turned out, on the pre-bonus 10.46 cr shares: FY25 (₹35.52) for dates in Jan-Mar 2024, FY26 (₹24.94) for FY25, our FY27E for FY26 and our FY28E for Apr-Sep 2026. **Trough rule:** no year is left out: FY26 EPS (₹24.94) is above half the best of the previous three years (₹17.8, half of FY25's ₹35.52), and so are FY27E (₹29.1) and FY28E. **Exceptional items** are immaterial (₹3.3 cr labour-code charge in FY26, ~1% of profit), so the base uses reported EPS; on Screener's wider "excluding exceptional" profit (which strips treasury and forex gains, ₹1.4 a share in FY26) the median is 54.9x. We multiply the median by the nine pharma peers' move over the same window (+10.7%) and round to the nearest half-turn. No blend with Concord's own move, no growth uplift.

blocks.h: The honest problem with this median

blocks.p: The rule uses EPS as it actually came in, so a year in which earnings fell unexpectedly shows up as a very high multiple. Concord's FY26 EPS fell 30%: during FY25 the market paid ₹1,452-2,601 a share expecting growth, which reads as 58.2-104.3x on the FY26 EPS that arrived (median 67.9x, 52 of the 144 points). The fall is not deep enough to count as a trough (it would have to halve), so the rule keeps it. Leaving those 52 weeks out gives **47.5x (₹1,900, +38.4%)**; using only points priced on FY27E/FY28E (from 1-Apr-2025) gives 53.5x (₹2,140). **Even these give a BUY**, because the window is dominated by FY25-FY26, when the market expected far more growth than came; the weeks priced on FY28E (Apr-Sep 2026) have a median of 35.6x, close to today's 37.5x. What would change the answer is the street's view of what Concord deserves (25-40x FY28E), which is a judgement our rule does not make.

blocks.callout: **Where Concord sits:** at 52.2x trailing EPS and 35.9x trailing EV/EBITDA, Concord is priced above generic API makers (Granules 35.6x, Ipca 35.6x) and near Neuland (55.0x), below the CDMOs (Divi's 82.8x, Anthem 81.6x, Sai Life 88.1x). Its margins (34.9% in FY26, 42% in FY25) are among the best in the group; its ROE (13.6%) is held down by cash and working capital.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a rare fermentation franchise after a bad year; the rule says BUY, the cash flows say be careful

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** one of few companies anywhere that can make immunosuppressant, oncology and anti-infective APIs by fermentation at scale, with a clean regulatory record, 74-79% gross margins, no debt and ₹442 cr of cash. FY26 was a bad year (revenue −12%, EPS −30%) for reasons management calls timing; Q1FY27 (+26% revenue) supports that. Against it: 58% of revenue from mature immunosuppressants, share gains bought with price, a formulation and injectable push that has so far cost ~₹48 cr a year, and cash that may go to acquisitions.

**What you are paying:** ₹1,374 is 52.2x trailing EPS, 37.5x our FY28E and 34.3x Sep-28E. On the street's method (P/E), Concord's own 54.9x median since Jan-2024, lifted by the pharma peers' +10.7% over the same window, gives 61x Sep-28E EPS: {{dcf.tp|inr}}, {{dcf.upside|chg}}, a **BUY**. We are uneasy with the size of that number: the median comes from a three-year history in which the market paid 58-104x the FY26 EPS that arrived; brokers use 25-40x (Choice's 40x is ₹1,600, +17%); and the DCF (₹695) needs ~24% growth for 15 years to justify even today's price. The BUY is robust to the window choice (every start date gives ≥ +38%), but not to the multiple the street thinks Concord deserves.

bullets: **Rating: BUY, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}), ₹1,220 after the 1:1 bonus.** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.
**The rule gives BUY below ~₹2,120**, HOLD between that and ~₹2,570, and SELL above it, on today's numbers.

**Biggest swing factor: the multiple.** Each 1x on the P/E is ~₹40 a share; each point of FY28-29E EBITDA margin ~₹1.1 of Sep-28E EPS (~₹68 a share at 61x). Leaving out the FY26-priced weeks gives 47.5x (₹1,900); the street's 40x gives ₹1,600.
**For a reviewer:** the BUY is the rule's answer, not a high-conviction call. The latest broker targets (median ₹1,400) and our own DCF both sit far below it.

A drug that damps the immune system, mainly so the body does not reject a transplanted organ (tacrolimus, mycophenolate, cyclosporine)
The finished medicine (tablet, capsule, injection) made from an API
Contract development and manufacturing for another company's (often an innovator's) molecule

A supplier a customer adds alongside its existing one, usually at a lower price

Good manufacturing practice certificates from the World Health Organization / European regulators
